rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad renders the recurring accusation against earlier messengers as calling them spellbinders or madmen.
rows.anchor: never yet came any apostle to those who lived before their time but they said

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: He frames the charge as inherited thinking, then explains the rejection as the people's overweening arrogance.
rows.anchor: perchance, handed down this [way of thinking] as a legacy unto one another? Nay

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad glosses the word translated “spellbinder” literally as “sorcerer.”
rows.anchor: Lit., "sorcerer".

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Most commentators classify the surah as Meccan, while Zamakhshari and Suyuti assign it to Medina.
rows.anchor: regard this surah as a Meccan revelation, Zamakhshari and (among the later scholars) Suyuti ascribe it to the Medina period

rows.speaker: Baydawi
rows.claim: Baydawi leaves the period open and allows that portions may precede and follow the Prophet's emigration to Medina.
rows.anchor: question open, and adds that parts of it may

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Some authorities place it just after surah 13, but Asad finds this unhelpful because surah 13 also cannot be dated confidently.
rows.anchor: Some authorities are of the opinion that it followed immediately upon surah 13 ("Thunder"): an opinion which is not very helpful

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: God raised the skies and established a measure for all things.
rows.anchor: And the skies has He raised high, and has devised [for all things] a measure

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The measure is a standard of right that people must not transgress.
rows.anchor: so that you [too, O men,] might never transgress the measure [of what is right)

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: People must weigh their deeds fairly and must not fall short of the measure.
rows.anchor: weigh, therefore, [your deed] with equity, and cut not the measure short!

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Following Zamakhshari, Asad reads mizan broadly as measure or measuring by any means, in concrete and abstract senses.
rows.anchor: The noun mizan, usually denoting a "balance", has here the more general connotation of "measure" or "measuring" by any means whatsoever (Zamakhshari)

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad links this parabolic use of mizan with 42:17 and 57:25.
rows.anchor: Cf. also the parabolic use of the term mza~ in 42:17 and 57:25.

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad dates the surah shortly after surah 67, around three or four years before the emigration to Medina.
rows.anchor: REVEALED shortly after surah 67 (Al-Mulk), i.e., about three or four years before the Prophet's exodus to Medina.

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad renders al-haqqah as the laying-bare of truth, emphasizes its awe, and says its reality exceeds human conception.
rows.anchor: OH, THE LAYING-BARE of the truth! [1] (69:2) How awesome that laying-bare of the truth! (69:3) And what could make thee conceive

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The translation says Thamud and Ad were overtaken by calamity: Thamud by upheaval, Ad by a storm lasting seven nights and eight days, leaving bodies like hollow palm trunks.
rows.anchor: Now as for the Thamud - they were destroyed by a violent upheaval [of the earth]

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The storm's victims lay like uprooted hollow palm trunks, with no remnant visible.
rows.anchor: thou couldst see those people laid low [in death], as though they were so many [uprooted] trunks of hollow palm trees

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The Day of Resurrection and Judgment will disclose the true quality of each person's past life and deeds, revealing the destiny those deeds entail.
rows.anchor: the Day of Resurrection and Judgment, on which man will become fully aware of the quality of his past life

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The ultimate reality will be beyond anticipation or imagination, which is why the rhetorical question receives no answer.
rows.anchor: this sudden perception of the ultimate reality will be beyond anything that man can anticipate or imagine: hence, no answer is given

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad supplies “with the female ovum” as the unstated counterpart in the description of the mixed drop.
rows.anchor: Sc., "with the female ovum"; cf. 86:6-7.

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: God has shown humanity the way, leaving each person to prove grateful or ungrateful.
rows.anchor: Verily, We have shown him the way: [4] [and it rests with him to prove himself] either grateful or ungrateful.

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Those who deny the truth face chains, shackles, and a blazing flame.
rows.anchor: for those who deny the truth [5] We have readied chains and shackles, and a blazing flame

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The virtuous drink from a blissful source, a cup scented with flowers that flows abundantly for God's servants.
rows.anchor: the truly virtuous shall drink from a cup flavoured with the calyx of sweet-smelling flowers

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Hearing and sight signify reason and instinctive moral discernment; God also guides people through revelation given to prophets.
rows.anchor: with "hearing and sight", i.e., with reason and the instinctive ability to discern between right and wrong, good and evil

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Many authorities, including Suyuti, regard the surah as the last Meccan revelation; some commentators assign the whole surah to Medina.
rows.anchor: among them Suyuti - regard th is surah as the last Meccan revelation.

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Authentic traditions cited by Tabari, Baghawi, and Ibn Kathir place at least the first four verses shortly after the Prophet's arrival in Medina.
rows.anchor: However, a number of authentic Traditions make it clear that at least the first four verses were

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Weighing the evidence, Asad assigns the main body to late Mecca and the opening to early Medina, making the surah a threshold between periods like surah 29.
rows.anchor: the main body of this surah indeed represents the very last Meccan revelation

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The condemned demand full measure when receiving from others but give less than their due when measuring or weighing what they owe.
rows.anchor: give less than what is due! [1]

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The warning extends beyond commerce to every practical and moral social relation, including each person's rights, obligations, and possessions.
rows.anchor: does not, of course, refer only to commercial dealings but touches upon every aspect of social relations, both practical and moral

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The wrongdoers are to be raised and called to account on the awesome Day when everyone stands before the Sustainer of all worlds.
rows.anchor: on an awesome Day (83:6) the Day when all men shall stand

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: A warning of grievous future suffering is excepted for those who repent, believe, and do good works, whose reward will be unending.
rows.anchor: unless it be such [of them] as [repent, and] attain to faith, and do good works: for theirs shall be a reward unending!

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Humanity is deeply ungrateful to God and bears witness to that ingratitude.
rows.anchor: VERILY, towards his Sustainer man is most ungrateful [3] (100:7) and to this, behold, he [himself] bears witness indeed

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The human being is ardently devoted to wealth.
rows.anchor: to the love of wealth is he most ardently devoted.

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: On the Last Day the dead will be raised, hidden thoughts exposed, and the Sustainer will show complete knowledge of people.
rows.anchor: all that is [hidden] in men's hearts

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: When people surrender to appetites symbolized by the charging horses, they forget God and their responsibility to Him.
rows.anchor: whenever he surrenders to his appetites, symbolized by the madly storming chargers, he forgets God and his own responsibility to Him

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Literally, the sinner's “mother” or goal is an abyss of suffering and despair; umm idiomatically means what embraces or enfolds.
rows.anchor: is used idiomatically to denote something that embraces or enfolds.

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad gives the literal sense as humanity being in a state of loss, except for those who meet the stated conditions.
rows.anchor: man is indeed in [a state of] loss, except those. . .

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The surah takes its conventional name from a noun in verse 1 and was probably revealed late in Muhammad's third year of prophethood.
rows.anchor: TAKING its conventional name from a noun

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad places it probably after surah 75, “Resurrection.”
rows.anchor: probably after surah 75 ("Resurrection").

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The surah condemns slander and fault-finding alongside amassing wealth and treating it as protection that will secure immortality.
rows.anchor: WOE unto every slanderer, fault-finder! [1] (104:2) [Woe unto him[2]] who amasses wealth and counts it a safeguard

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The hoarder instead faces crushing torment: God's fire rises over guilty hearts and closes around them in endless columns.
rows.anchor: which will rise over the [guilty] hearts:[5]

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad inserts the repeated “Woe unto him” because verses 2–3 describe a blameworthy attitude distinct from the two types in verse 1.
rows.anchor: This repetitive interpolation is necessary because the blameworthy attitude spoken of in verses 2-3 obviously belongs to a category entirely different

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Counting wealth as a safeguard is a metonym for treating material acquisition as almost religious, displacing spiritual concerns.
rows.anchor: a metonym for the tendency to attribute an almost "religious" value to the acquisition and possession of material goods

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad bases his rendering of addadahu as “counts it a safeguard” on Jawhari's lexical explanation.
rows.anchor: My rendering of 'addadahu in the preceding verse as "[he] counts it a safeguard" is based on Jawhari's explanation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For kanud, consult WKAS under the root k-n-d; the implied ingratitude also appears in early Meccan 80:17.
rows.anchor: Zum hier implizierten Gedanken der Undankbarkeit vgl. frühmekkanisch auch 80:17.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An ʾinsan saying delays the eschatological resolution of the enigmatic oath opening; Neuwirth calls the saying a motif that later becomes a topos.
rows.anchor: Die eschatologische Auflösung der enigmatischen Schwureinleitung wird durch einen – später zum Topos werdenden – ʾinsān-Spruch retardiert

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 6–8 form the surah's structural center and contrast with the dynamic verbal and participial clauses around them; these are its only nominal sentences.
rows.anchor: Sprachlich stehen V. 6–8, welche die strukturelle Mitte der Sure bilden, in deutlichem Kontrast zur dynamischen Aufgewühltheit von V. 1–5 und V. 9–11

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage accuses humanity of publicly bearing witness to ingratitude toward God in verses 6–7 and of possessiveness in verse 8.
rows.anchor: Inhaltlich werden dem Menschen eine öffentlich „Bezeugung“ von Undank gegen Gott (V. 6–7) sowie Besitzgier (V. 8) vorgeworfen.

rows.speaker: Neuwirth
rows.claim: Neuwirth reads these failings as examples of pre-Islamic anthropocentric values.
rows.anchor: Neuwirth sieht hierin exemplarische Stellvertreter für den anthropozentrischen Wertekanon der vorislamischen Zeit

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The text does not explicitly criticize particular pre-Islamic Arab virtues.
rows.anchor: doch kritisiert der Text nicht ausdrücklich bestimmte altarabische Tugenden.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording parallels 69:21 and 88:9; other early Meccan uses of r-d-y occur at 93:5, 92:21, 89:28, and 53:26, giving the root an apparently consistent eschatological association.
rows.anchor: Die Wurzel ist offenbar durchgängig eschatologisch konnotiert.

rows.speaker: Fischer
rows.claim: Fischer reads the phrase idiomatically as a wish that one's mother fall, a euphemism for perishing.
rows.anchor: Idiomatisch: „Seine Mutter stürzt“ = „Seine Mutter möge dem Fall preisgegeben sein“ – „eine Art Euphemismus für einfaches halaka ‚der geht zu Grunde’“ (so Fischer 1906, 41).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The topological reading takes hawiya as a gorge or abyss, hence Hell; lexicographers support the equivalence with mahwa or mahwat.
rows.anchor: Topologisch: „Seine Mutter ist ein Schlund, Abgrund“, wobei hāwiya ein Synonym für mahwā bzw. mahwāt

rows.speaker: Fischer
rows.claim: Fischer prefers the idiom; the author acknowledges its supporting evidence but finds a purely idiomatic reading difficult because the next teaching question should refer to hawiya.
rows.anchor: Zugunsten der von August Fischer präferierten Deutung des Verses im Sinne des Idioms hawat ʾummuhū spricht

rows.speaker: Fischer
rows.claim: Fischer even treats verses 10–11 as a later addition to preserve the idiomatic reading; the author considers this an unsupported textual split.
rows.anchor: Fischer geht deshalb sogar so weit, V. 10.11 für einen späteren Zusatz zu halten

rows.speaker: Paret
rows.claim: Paret makes hiya refer nonspecifically to the preceding statement as a whole, but the author rejects this as inconsistent with the usual concrete referent and feminine pronoun.
rows.anchor: Parets Übersetzung von V. 10 („Doch wie kannst du wissen, was das bedeutet?“) ist offensichtlich bemüht

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dictionary equivalences between hawiya and mahwa or mahwat are not confined to explanations of this Quranic verse, supporting an independent lexical basis.
rows.anchor: die Gleichsetzung von hāwiya mit mahwā bzw. mahwāt in den Wörterbüchern gerade nicht im Zusammenhang mit 101:9 behandelt wird

rows.speaker: Sells
rows.claim: Sells objects that early Arabic attestations for hawiya meaning abyss are tenuous; the author answers that lexicographical evidence and rhyme support the word.
rows.anchor: dass „attestations for the term hāwiya meaning abyss in early Arabic are tenuous“ (Sells 1993, 418), greift angesichts der lexikographischen Belege nicht

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The topological reading is reinforced by Hell as abyss in Revelation 9:1,11 and by Quranic teaching questions about obscure place names in 83:7–8 and 83:18–19; an intended echo of the idiom may coexist.
rows.anchor: Die topologische Deutung von hāwiya wird überdies dadurch bestätigt, dass die Hölle auch in der Offenbarung des Johannes 9:1.11 als „Abgrund“ bezeichnet wird

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some commentators gloss hawiya as a proper name for Hell, but this likely secondary interpretation entered the lexicons.
rows.anchor: manche islamische Kommentatoren hāwiya einfach als einen Eigennamen für die Hölle aufzufassen

rows.speaker: Torrey
rows.claim: Torrey derives hawiya from Hebrew howa, “destruction”; the author doubts early Meccan listeners knew a term found only twice in the Hebrew Bible.
rows.anchor: Torrey zufolge handelt es sich bei hāwiya um eine Arabisierung von hebr. hōwā, „Verderben“

rows.speaker: Bellamy
rows.claim: Bellamy emends the consonantal text to fa-ummatun hāwiya, “a steep downward path”; the author notes no such variant is attested and calls it an easier secondary reading.
rows.anchor: Bellamy 1992 plädiert dafür, den rasm von V. 9 als fa-ʾummatun hāwiya („ein steiler Weg nach unten“) zu emendieren.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The construction about mutual exhortation echoes 90:17, and the phrase about believers and good works is characteristic of late Meccan and Medinan texts; the verb amana is cross-referenced at 69:33.
rows.anchor: Vgl. 90:17 (ṯumma kāna mina llaḏīna ʾāmanū wa-tawāṣau bi-ṣ-ṣabri wa-tawāṣau bi-l-marḥamah).

rows.speaker: Medina II
rows.claim: Medina II places a verse divider after haqq, yielding rhyme but separating two parallel, conceptually linked clauses, which Neuwirth objects to.
rows.anchor: Medina II setzt einen Verstrenner nach ḥaqq (Spitaler, Verszählung, 35). Dabei ergäbe sich zwar ein Reim

rows.speaker: Neuwirth
rows.claim: Neuwirth argues that the proposed divider separates two parallel clauses that belong together in thought.
rows.anchor: zwei gedanklich zusammengehörende und parallel gebaute Satzteile getrennt (Neuwirth, Studien, 35).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because verse 3 is probably a later addition, its unusual length is unsurprising.
rows.anchor: Da V. 3 vermutlich ein späterer Zusatz ist (s. o.), ist die übermäßige Länge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Woe formulas followed by vice catalogues also occur at 107:4–7, 83:1–3, 83:10–11, 52:11–12, and 51:60; 83:1–6 is especially close in its wealth theme and following rhetorical question.
rows.anchor: Durch wail eingeleitete Wehsprüche mit folgendem Lasterkatalog finden sich sonst noch in 107:4–7, 83:1–3, 83:10.11 und 52:11.12

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Woe speeches as a basic form of prophetic discourse already appear in the Hebrew Bible, for example Micah 2:1–3.
rows.anchor: Wehsprüche als grundlegende Form prophetischer Rede begegnen bereits in der Hebräischen Bibel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The perfect in “gathered wealth and counted it” is aspectual, which motivates translating it with the German present tense.
rows.anchor: Da es sich um ein aspektuelles Perfekt handeln dürfte (vgl. die Anmerkung zu 96:1.2), wurde mit dem deutschen Präsens übersetzt.

rows.speaker: Neuwirth
rows.claim: Neuwirth once proposed adding the question particle to yahsabu because the other four early Meccan uses have it and 83:1–6 offers a parallel woe followed by a polemical question; she later seems to withdraw the emendation.
rows.anchor: hat Neuwirth dafür argumentiert, yaḥsabu in 104:4 zu ʾa-yaḥsabu zu emendieren (Neuwirth, Studien, 233 f.). In ihrer jüngsten Veröffentlichung scheint sie jedoch

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pursuit of immortality, khuld, is a motif of pre-Islamic poetry; Neuwirth cites Tarafa's Muallaqa verse 54 as evidence.
rows.anchor: Das Streben nach „Ewigkeit“ bzw. „Unsterblichkeit“ (ḫuld) ist ein Motiv der altarabischen Dichtung

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening woe, vice list, and insult sketch a prototypical sinner who trusts without basis that money grants immortality, driving antisocial conduct and limitless accumulation.
rows.anchor: Der einleitende Wehspruch mit Lasterkatalog (V. 1.2) sowie das anschließende Scheltwort entwerfen das Charakterporträt eines prototypischen Sünders.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This hoarding is the opposite of ostentatious spending criticized at 90:6, yet both reflect the delusion that people can secure immortality by their own power.
rows.anchor: Das kritisierte Verhalten bildet damit das genaue Gegenteil der in 90:6 angeprangerten ostentativen Besitzverschwendung

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 4 counters the imagined immortality with punishment: instead of living forever, the sinner is shattered in Hell, expressed by the root h-t-m.
rows.anchor: Das Handeln des Getadelten hat gerade nicht seine Unsterblichkeit zur Folge, sondern zieht im Gegenteil seine „Zertrümmerung“ (ḥ-ṭ-m) in der Hölle nach sich.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unusual fuʿala form for Hell recalls verse 1's same form for vice: the slanderer who harms others in life is harmed in the afterlife, linking deed and retribution.
rows.anchor: Während er im Diesseits durch sein verleumderisches Verhalten andere schädigt, wird er im Jenseits als Strafe dafür selbst geschädigt
